summary: An April 1st joke RFC. It describes the Faster than LIght speed Protocol (FLIP), which supposedly uses artificial intelligence to predict future packets at the receiving end before they arrive, avoiding congestion and delivering faster. It is humor, not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9564 is an April 1st joke proposing that an AI predict packets before they arrive. It presents the idea as a protocol called FLIP, with a header and commands.

questions: what is the faster than light speed protocol
subtitle: An April 1st proposal claims AI can predict packets before they arrive.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke imagines using AI predictions to avoid network delay and congestion, including for communications with long distances.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes FLIP, in which peers prepare trained language models and a receiver predicts future packets based on a shared model.
tldr.outcome: The RFC presents packet prediction as faster-than-light delivery. Its protocol format and claims are part of a humorous document, not a real Internet standard.

today: RFC 9564 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2024. Its faster-than-light packet prediction proposal is humorous and does not describe a deployed networking technology.

sections.title: The Faster-Than-Light Idea
sections.content: RFC 9564 proposes the Faster than LIght speed Protocol (FLIP). It claims that a large language model could predict future packets at the receiving peer before they arrive. The document applies this idea to networking at different layers, including a hypothetical use for deep-space communication.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke says an AI can guess a packet before it arrives, making communication seem faster than light. The document presents this as the purpose of FLIP.

sections.title: The FLIP Header
sections.content: The proposed FLIP shim header contains Version, Command, Inner Protocol, and Optional Data fields. The Version field holds a SHA-256 hash of the model. The RFC leaves header and field lengths unspecified, saying the receiving neural network is expected to determine where the header ends.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed header names a model version, a command, an inner protocol, and optional data. The joke says the receiver's model will work out where the header ends.

sections.title: The Two Commands
sections.content: The document defines a model command with codepoint 0x01 and a data command with codepoint 0x02. The model command carries a trained model in optional data. The data command tells the receiving peer that following data can be predicted. The RFC notes that sending a model may reveal it to an observer.
sections.plainLanguage: The model command sends a model, while the data command marks data that the receiver can predict. The RFC also jokes about risks from disclosing a model.
